headline: Consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in August; the Fed meets Tuesday and Wednesday

items.title: Consumer Price Index, August 2026
items.summary: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4 percent in August on a seasonally adjusted basis, and 3.4 percent over the twelve months ending in August before seasonal adjustment. Leaving out food and energy, the index rose 0.3 percent in the month and 2.4 percent over the year. The energy index rose 2.1 percent in August and 16.3 percent over twelve months; the food index rose 0.1 percent; shelter rose 0.3 percent in the month and 3.0 percent over the year.
items.meaning: The CPI measures the average change in the prices that urban consumers pay for a basket of goods and services. A 3.4 percent yearly rise means a basket that cost $100 a year earlier cost about $103.40 in August. Most of the gap between the headline and the ex-food-and-energy figure is energy.

items.title: Producer Price Index, August 2026
items.summary: The Producer Price Index for final demand moved up 0.4 percent in August, seasonally adjusted, and rose 5.4 percent for the twelve months ended in August on an unadjusted basis. The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.3 percent in the month and 4.7 percent over the year.
items.meaning: The PPI measures the average change in the selling prices that U.S. producers receive for their goods and services. Producer price changes do not pass through to consumer prices one for one, and the two indexes cover different baskets, but a persistent gap between producer and consumer inflation is one of the things economists watch.

source.documentTitle: Producer Price Index News Release — August 2026

items.title: Employment Situation, August 2026
items.summary: Released the week before: total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 162,000 in August and the unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.1 percent. Average hourly earnings for private-sector employees rose 10 cents, or 0.3 percent, in the month and 3.1 percent over the year. The labor force participation rate edged up to 61.6 percent.
items.meaning: Payroll growth of 162,000 with the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.1 percent describes a labor market that added jobs while the share of the labor force without a job held steady. With average hourly earnings up 3.1 percent and consumer prices up 3.4 percent over the same twelve months, pay rose less than the CPI.

sections.title: One concept to know
sections.text: Headline inflation is the change in the whole CPI basket. Core inflation leaves out food and energy, whose prices swing with harvests and oil markets. Neither is more real than the other: households pay headline prices, but core is a steadier read on the underlying trend. In August the two differed by a full percentage point over the year — 3.4 percent against 2.4 percent — and energy accounted for most of the gap.
